finding_details.summary: Mappings merged after the bounded shutdown join are never removed
finding_details.evidence: _release_ports sets _ports_cancel and joins the ports-open thread for at most discovery_timeout_s + request_timeout_s. If the thread is still alive after that, it only logs a warning. It then takes a snapshot of _upnp_retained (line 2125) and deletes only that snapshot. A thread that finishes later still runs _merge_opening, which adds entries to _upnp_retained (line 2104), but nothing deletes them, so those router mappings stay up until the lease ends (up to 2 h). Normally the cancel-at-each-request-boundary design keeps the thread within the join budget. It can overrun when there is scheduling delay, or when connect() plus the deadline reader together take slightly more than request_timeout_s. Confirm with a fake IGD that delays its answer to just past the join budget.

finding_details.summary: The first SSDP responder on the LAN is trusted as the gateway, and its 'public address' is prefilled into the invite field
finding_details.evidence: discover() returns the first readable 200 reply from any peer. _same_host only checks that LOCATION points back to that same responder, not that the responder is the default gateway. Any LAN host can therefore answer the M-SEARCH, receive the SOAP calls, and return any global IPv4 from GetExternalIPAddress. _public() accepts that value, and ui/app.js prefillAddress() puts it into #f-address. One click on 'Use this address' then sends the guest to an attacker-chosen host. The R5 click gate and the global-IP filter limit the impact, but the trust assumption is not written down anywhere. Comparing the responder with the default-route gateway, or labelling the prefilled value as unverified, would close or document the gap. Inference: this depends on the threat model in the spec, which I did not re-read.

finding_details.summary: A 'mapped' result outlives its lease and carries into rematch lobbies
finding_details.evidence: _ports_opening is never reset when a phase or lobby changes. Only a new click or shutdown changes it. The lease is fixed at 2 h from the click, with no renewal (MAX_LEASE_S, lease_s=7200), and a duel lasts up to MAX_DURATION_S = 3600 s. A rematch lobby opened after the lease has run out still shows 'Ports … are open until HH:MM' (ui/app.js portsBlock) with a time already past, plus the old address. The host may then think the ports are still open while the router has already dropped them. A fix: _ports_view could show the status as expired once clock() > expires_at, or the status could reset when a new lobby opens.

finding_details.summary: expires_at is counted from the click, not from AddPortMapping
finding_details.evidence: _merge_opening sets expires_at = click + lease_s, but the router's lease starts when each AddPortMapping is accepted, which can be several seconds later (discovery plus up to six requests). The shown expiry is therefore slightly early. That is the safe direction, but the code does not say so, and the three mappings do not expire at the same moment.

finding_details.summary: Discovery takes the first IGD reply, which may be the wrong box on double-NAT or mesh networks
finding_details.evidence: If several IGDs answer (an ISP box plus the user's own router, or mesh nodes), whichever replies first is used. On double NAT this can open the ports on the inner router only. The NOTE_NOT_PUBLIC path partly signals this, because GetExternalIPAddress then returns a private address, but nothing filters by the default route. This is a deployment assumption that should be documented under known limits.

finding_details.summary: Retained mapping on an earlier gateway is overwritten (and never removed) when a later opening maps the same couple on a different gateway
finding_details.evidence: `_upnp_retained` is keyed by (port, protocol) only; `_merge_opening` does `self._upnp_retained[(port, proto)] = gateway`. If opening #1 maps 3 couples on gateway A and opening #2 (network change, or a different IGD answering SSDP first) maps the same couples on gateway B, A's records are replaced, so `_release_ports` only deletes on B and A's mappings stay open until the lease expires (≤ 7200 s). The comment at the field definition says each record is 'lié à la passerelle qui l'a posé', and R6 asks to remove 'chaque mapping posé par le service et encore réputé actif'. The keying keeps the R6 bound of 'au plus trois mappings', so this may be an accepted trade-off, but it is not documented; at minimum log the dropped gateway's couples, or key by (gateway, couple) and keep the 3-expiry bound by other means.

finding_details.summary: An opening thread that outlives the shutdown join merges mappings after the retained snapshot; they are never removed and the warning does not name them
finding_details.evidence: `_release_ports` sets cancel, joins for discovery_timeout_s + request_timeout_s, logs 'port opening still running at shutdown' if still alive, then snapshots `_upnp_retained`. A thread that finishes later (e.g. a slow GC pause, or connect() + deadline overrun at the edge) still calls `_merge_opening` under the lock and adds retained couples that nobody deletes. The daemon thread is then killed at process exit. The impact is bounded by the lease, but the spec's 'Un échec de suppression est consigné' is not met for these couples. A fix could be to read `_ports_opening`/retained after the join only when the thread is dead, and otherwise log the couples of the in-flight opening as possibly left open.

finding_details.summary: Discovery stops at the first readable SSDP 200 reply without checking ST, so a non-IGD responder can mask the real gateway
finding_details.evidence: `discover` returns the first datagram for which `_location` finds a LOCATION. It does not check that the reply's `ST` matches `SEARCH_TARGET`, and it does not collect other replies. Some LAN devices answer every M-SEARCH, and a mesh node or second router can also answer. If one of them replies first, `find_gateway` fails with `no_service` or `foreign_control_url`, and the real IGD that answers 50 ms later is ignored. Checking `ST` in `_location`, or trying later replies until the deadline after a description fails, would make this more robust. The fake IGD tests use a single responder, so they don't cover this case.

finding_details.summary: `open_ports` can raise on malformed `ports` despite the 'Aucune exception ne sort' contract
finding_details.evidence: `_couples(ports)` (unpacking) and `_ports_ok` (`set(couples)`) run before the `try`. An element that is not a pair raises ValueError/TypeError, and an unhashable port (e.g. a list) raises TypeError from `set()`. `delete_mappings` has the same problem: `_couples(mappings)` is outside its try. The engine always passes well-formed int/str tuples, so this can't happen today, but the docstring makes a module-wide guarantee.

finding_details.summary: MX is derived as max(1, int(timeout_s)), which can exceed the discovery deadline or the UDA cap of 5
finding_details.evidence: With discovery_timeout_s = 0.5, MX = 1, so devices may legitimately delay their reply past the 0.5 s deadline. With a large timeout (e.g. 30), MX = 30, which is outside the UDA 1.1 range of 1–5. The shipped value (2) is fine; clamping MX to [1, min(5, floor(timeout_s))] would make other configurations behave as intended.
